1	# Planetfall — Plan & Status
2	
3	_Last updated: 2026-06-05_
4	
5	## The pitch
6	
7	You're a stranded astronaut. Your ship's AI has **amnesia** — it lost all its
8	context about what happened. To escape, you explore a 3D planet, find debris,
9	and each piece hides a small puzzle solved by **recovering lost context**.
10	
11	The hook: reconstructing the ship's memory in-fiction **is the same act** as
12	recovering a real codebase's history with [Entire](https://docs.entire.io).
13	Each puzzle teaches a real `entire` command.
14	
15	> Note: `entire explain` does **not** exist (it was an early guess). The real
16	> context-recovery commands are `recap`, `checkpoint`, `activity`, `dispatch`.
17	
18	## Locked decisions
19	
20	- **3D, web-based.** Three.js + Vite, no downloaded assets — the planet is
21	  generated procedurally at load.
22	- **Planet look (approved):** a dreamy **lavender ocean world** with a few
23	  **gold metallic islands** that shimmer, wrapped in a **Saturn-style ring**.
24	  Soft, minimal, calm.
25	  - NOT earthlike. NOT the glowing-magenta-"neural"-vein look (tried it; it
26	    looked "itchy" — busy land texture fighting bright veins. Removed.)
27	  - Keep lighting (sun / ambient / env) **low** — the lavender sea washes out
28	    white if over-lit.
29	- **Build order:** get the world feeling right **first** (done), then puzzles,
30	  then the command engine + win/lose.
31	- **Two-level structure (approved 2026-06-05):** the game is two views, not one.
32	  - **Orbit view** — bird's-eye planet; click a marked **island hotspot** to land.
33	  - **Island view** — a **walkable, first-person** landscape (WASD + mouse-look);
34	    artifacts are embedded **in the terrain**, not floating on the globe. Walk up
35	    to one and press **E** to inspect; **B** leaves back to orbit.
36	  - Transition is a **crossfade cut** into a dedicated island scene (not a
37	    seamless dive onto the sphere).
38	  - Starting with **one island holding all the artifacts/puzzles**; more later.
39	
40	## Status
41	
42	### Done ✅ — the 3D world (user-approved)
43	- Procedural planet: lavender ocean, gold **metallic** islands (PBR
44	  metalness + low roughness + `RoomEnvironment` IBL → shimmer), soft frost
45	  poles, drifting clouds.
46	- Saturn-style banded ring (tilted, two gaps, transparent).
47	- Soft lavender fresnel atmosphere, violet-tinted starfield.
48	- Orbit + zoom controls; slow auto-rotation.
49	- Verified rendering in headless Chrome (WebGL2), no console errors.
50	
51	### Done ✅ — the two-level flow (2026-06-05)
52	- **Orbit view** (`planetView.js`): the planet plus a clean **HTML map pin**
53	  ("LANDING SITE") that tracks the island in screen space — no glow/beam. On
54	  hover a thin **outline ring** fades in on the surface and the pin lifts; click
55	  (pin or island) → crossfade → island. The island is found via a shared
56	  elevation sampler, and the **camera frames it front-and-centre on load**. Pin
57	  hides when the island rotates to the far side.
58	- **Island view** (`islandView.js`): a procedural **walkable terrain** island
59	  (radial-falloff heightmap, gold highlands, surrounded by lavender sea),
60	  lavender-dusk sky, soft warm sun. **First-person** controller (`firstPerson.js`,
61	  PointerLockControls + WASD, glued to the terrain, clamped to the island).
62	- The 4 artifacts (reusing the `debris.js` prop builders) sit **in the terrain**
63	  with tall findable light-beams; walk within range → "Press E to inspect" →
64	  opens the shared fragment panel. **B** returns to orbit.
65	- Verified both views render in headless Chrome (WebGL2), no console errors.
66	
67	### Not built yet ⏳
68	- Puzzle mechanics (panels are still lore stubs only).
69	- The command engine (see open questions).
70	- Win/lose + checkpoint-collection state.
71	- More islands (only one is built; orbit view shows a single pin).
72	- Polish backlog: bloom on gold glints, ring shadow cast on planet; island
73	  pass — props/landmarks so the terrain reads less like empty dunes, water
74	  shader, a proper skybox, third-person option if wanted; tune the in-terrain
75	  artifact beam tint (reads pink over the lavender sky).
76	
77	## Puzzle design (PROPOSED — not yet reviewed/built)
78	
79	Arc: **orient → restore → understand → escape**. Each puzzle is small: run a
80	command → read the recovered context → use one detail from it.
81	
82	| # | Fragment | Command | What's lost | Puzzle |
83	|---|----------|-----------|-------------|--------|
84	| 1 | 🪖 EVA Helmet | `recap` | "What was I doing before the crash?" | Run `recap`; read the summary of recent log entries; pick out the mission. |
85	| 2 | 📖 Torn Logbook | `checkpoint` | A setting got corrupted in the crash | Search checkpoints, find the last good one before the corruption, rewind to it. |
86	| 3 | 🖥️ Nav Panel | `activity` | "*When* did it go wrong?" | Read the activity timeline; find when the anomaly started. |
87	| 4 | 📡 Signal Beacon | `dispatch` | No way to call for help | Generate a dispatch summarizing all recovered context, broadcast it → **win**. |
88	
89	- **#4 is the ending**: you can only send a complete dispatch after recovering
90	  the other three. This quietly answers "how do you win / how do checkpoints
91	  accumulate."
92	
93	### Open questions (decide before/while building puzzles)
94	1. **Does the arc + mapping feel right?** (e.g. helmet → recap)
95	2. **Command engine:** simulated in-game terminal (portable, shareable web demo)
96	   vs. real CLI execution (authentic, needs a local backend) vs. hybrid.
97	   _Leaning simulated for a shareable demo; not yet decided._
98	3. **How literal is the command output?** Real-ish `entire` output vs. softened
99	   ship-AI flavor text.
100	4. **Win/lose model:** currently leaning "restore the ship's log" (collect all
101	   fragments, no hard lose state). Oxygen/timer and branching endings were
102	   other options.
103	
104	### Next step
105	Fully design **#1 (EVA Helmet / `recap`)** end-to-end as the template, then
106	clone the pattern to the other three.
107	
108	## Architecture / where things live
109	
110	```
111	index.html         # canvas + HUD + crossfade overlay + FP prompt + panel + loader
112	src/style.css      # HUD / panel / loader / fade / crosshair / FP-prompt styling
113	src/main.js        # VIEW MANAGER: owns renderer + resize + shared panel + the
114	                   #   render loop; crossfades between the two views.
115	                   #   ?view=island jumps straight onto the island (dev aid).
116	src/planetView.js  # orbit view: scene/lighting/stars/planet/clouds/atmo/ring +
117	                   #   the clickable gold landing hotspot. onIslandClick callback.
118	src/islandView.js  # island level: sky/light, terrain+water, the artifacts, the
119	                   #   proximity "press E" interaction. enter()/exit()/onExit.
120	src/terrain.js     # procedural island heightmap mesh + water + heightAt(x,z)
121	src/firstPerson.js # PointerLockControls + WASD walker, glued to the terrain
122	src/noise.js       # seedable 3D simplex + fBm (sphere-sampled → seamless)
123	src/planet.js      # bakes planet maps; createElevationSampler() finds land for
124	                   #   the hotspot. Palette constants (DEEP/SHALLOW/SNOW) here.
125	src/atmosphere.js  # fresnel limb-glow shell shader (orbit view)
126	src/ring.js        # procedural banded ring (radial-remapped UVs)
127	src/debris.js      # FRAGMENTS[] (lore + command) + exported prop BUILDERS,
128	                   #   reused as the island artifacts. createDebris() is now
129	                   #   unused (kept for reference / git history).
130	```
131	
132	Run: `npm install` then `npm run dev` → http://localhost:5173
133	Controls: orbit = drag/scroll, click the gold marker to land. Island = click to
134	capture mouse, WASD to walk, E to inspect a glowing artifact, B to leave.
135	
136	## History
137	Repo started as `signalkit` (a Python telemetry CLI), then pivoted to Planetfall
138	on 2026-06-05. The old code is recoverable via git history + Entire checkpoints.
139

> AGENT

I have a clear picture. Here's what this project is.

## Planetfall — a 3D browser game that teaches Entire commands

**The concept.** You're a stranded astronaut whose ship's AI has *amnesia* — it lost all its context. To escape, you explore a procedurally-generated 3D planet, find crash debris, and each artifact hides a small puzzle solved by **recovering lost context**. The fictional act of rebuilding the ship's memory *is the same act* as recovering a real codebase's history with [Entire](https://docs.entire.io) — so each puzzle teaches a real `entire` command: `recap`, `checkpoint`, `activity`, `dispatch`.

**Tech.** Three.js + Vite, no downloaded assets — the planet, islands, terrain, ring, and atmosphere are all generated at load from a seedable simplex/fBm noise field. Run with `npm install && npm run dev` → http://localhost:5173 (`?view=island` jumps straight onto the island).

**Two-level structure** (both done & user-approved):
- **Orbit view** (`planetView.js`) — bird's-eye of a dreamy lavender ocean world with shimmering gold metallic islands and a Saturn-style ring. An HTML map pin tracks a landing site; click to crossfade down.
- **Island view** (`islandView.js`) — a walkable first-person landscape (PointerLock + WASD, glued to procedural terrain). 4 artifacts sit in the terrain with light-beams; walk up and press **E** to inspect, **B** to return to orbit.

**Architecture** — `main.js` is the view manager (renderer, render loop, crossfade); `noise.js`/`planet.js`/`terrain.js` do the procedural generation; `debris.js` holds `FRAGMENTS[]` (lore + command mapping) and reusable prop builders.

### Where it stands
- ✅ **Done & approved:** the full 3D world and the orbit→island flow, verified rendering in headless Chrome with no console errors. Most recent commits added music controls and refined the landing marker.
- ⏳ **Not built yet:** the actual puzzle mechanics (panels are lore stubs), the **command engine** (simulated in-browser terminal vs. real CLI — *undecided, gates everything*), win/lose + checkpoint-collection state, and more islands.

### Two loose ends from the last session (per HANDOFF.md)
1. **Uncommitted `src/style.css` change** — the landing pin was recolored warm gold → cool cyan. The handoff flags this as needing a **decision**: it diverges from the locked "gold islands" theme. Confirm direction before committing or revert.
2. **`.codex/` (untracked)** — agent tooling config, not game code; decide gitignore vs. commit.

1	---
2	title: Quickstart
3	description: Get started with Entire by creating your first checkpoint.
4	---
5	
6	This quickstart walks you from installing Entire to creating your first checkpoint: a record of the prompts, transcript, tool calls, and file changes behind an AI-assisted commit.
7	
8	## Prerequisites
9	
10	- Git installed and configured
11	- An AI coding agent installed, such as Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Factory Droid, Gemini CLI, or OpenCode
12	- macOS, Linux, or Windows
13	- Optional: GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and authenticated, if you want Entire to create and push a private GitHub repository during setup
14	
15	## 1. Install Entire
16	
17	Entire ships two release channels:
18	
19	- `stable`: recommended for most users.
20	- `nightly`: prerelease builds with newer changes.
21	
22	Nightly is available through Homebrew and the Linux install script. Scoop currently supports stable only.
23	
24	<Tabs>
25	  <Tab title="macOS (Homebrew)">
26	    ```bash
27	    # Stable
28	    brew tap entireio/tap
29	    brew install --cask entire
30	
31	    # Nightly
32	    brew tap entireio/tap
33	    brew install --cask entire@nightly
34	    ```
35	  </Tab>
36	  <Tab title="Linux">
37	    ```bash
38	    # Stable
39	    curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
40	
41	    # Nightly
42	    curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
43	    ```
44	  </Tab>
45	  <Tab title="Windows (Scoop)">
46	    ```bash
47	    scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git
48	    scoop install entire/cli
49	    ```
50	  </Tab>
51	  <Tab title="From Source">
52	    ```bash
53	    go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
54	    ```
55	  </Tab>
56	</Tabs>
57	
58	Verify the installation:
59	
60	```bash
61	entire version
62	```
63	
64	## 2. Create a Demo Project
65	
66	```bash
67	mkdir entire-demo
68	cd entire-demo
69	```
70	
71	<Note>
72	Already in a Git repository? Skip this step and run the remaining commands from the repository root.
73	</Note>
74	
75	## 3. Enable Entire
76	
77	Choose the agent you already use. This example uses Codex; replace `codex` with your agent from the table below.
78	
79	```bash
80	entire enable -y --agent codex
81	```
82	
83	| Agent | Setup flag | Start command |
84	| --- | --- | --- |
85	| Claude Code | `--agent claude-code` | `claude` |
86	| Codex | `--agent codex` | `codex` |
87	| Copilot CLI | `--agent copilot-cli` | `copilot` |
88	| Cursor | `--agent cursor` | `cursor` |
89	| Factory Droid | `--agent factoryai-droid` | `droid` |
90	| Gemini CLI | `--agent gemini` | `gemini` |
91	| OpenCode | `--agent opencode` | `opencode` |
92	
93	This installs Git hooks that capture checkpoints when you commit and installs hook configuration for your selected agent. It also creates a `.entire/` directory for project and local settings.
94	
95	For shared projects, commit `.entire/settings.json` and `.entire/.gitignore`. See [Project and local files](/cli/configuration#project-and-local-files) for what can stay local.
96	
97	<Note>
98	Because this starts in a new folder, `entire enable -y` initializes Git and creates an initial commit. If `gh` is installed and authenticated, Entire can also create a private GitHub repository and push the initial commit.
99	</Note>
100	
101	## 4. Start an Agent Session
102	
103	Start the agent you selected:
104	
105	```bash
106	# Example with Claude Code
107	claude
108	
109	# Example with Codex
110	codex
111	
112	# Example with Copilot CLI
113	copilot
114	
115	# Example with Cursor
116	cursor
117	
118	# Example with Factory Droid
119	droid
120	
121	# Example with Gemini CLI
122	gemini
123	
124	# Example with OpenCode
125	opencode
126	```
127	
128	Prompt it to make a small change:
129	
130	```text
131	Create a file named hello-entire.md with a short note explaining that this repo is my first Entire checkpoint demo.
132	```
133	
134	When the agent finishes, exit the agent session if needed.
135	
136	## 5. Commit the Change
137	
138	Check what changed:
139	
140	```bash
141	git status
142	```
143	
144	Then commit it:
145	
146	```bash
147	git add hello-entire.md
148	git commit -m "Add first Entire demo file"
149	```
150	
151	Because Entire detected recent agent work, it may ask whether to link this commit to the session context:
152	
153	```text
154	Entire: Active Codex session detected
155	  Last prompt: Create a file named hello-entire.md with a short note...
156	
157	Link this commit to session context?
158	  [Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways (remember my choice):
159	```
160	
161	Press `Enter` or type `y` to link the commit. After the commit succeeds, you have created your first checkpoint.
162	
163	<Note>
164	If you choose `always`, Entire remembers that preference and links future matching commits automatically.
165	</Note>
166	
167	## 6. View Your First Checkpoint
168	
169	```bash
170	entire checkpoint list
171	```
172	
173	You should see the checkpoint linked to your commit.
174	
175	Entire stores permanent checkpoint data on a Git branch named:
176	
177	```text
178	entire/checkpoints/v1
179	```
180	
181	Your working branch stays clean. Entire does not add extra commits to it.
182	
183	## 7. Optional: Push Your Code and Checkpoint
184	
185	If your repository has a remote, push your code:
186	
187	```bash
188	git push
189	```
190	
191	Entire's pre-push hook also syncs checkpoint data to `entire/checkpoints/v1`.
192	
193	<Note>
194	Checkpoint data can include session context. If your repository is public, pushed checkpoint history is public too. See [Security & Privacy](/security) and [Checkpoint Remote](/cli/checkpoints#checkpoint-remote).
195	</Note>
196

208	  </Card>

210	    Set up your AI coding agent
211	  </Card>

1	---
2	title: Checkpoints
3	description: How Entire captures your AI coding sessions
4	---
5	
6	Entire captures AI coding sessions as you work, and creates permanent checkpoints when you make Git commits.
7	
8	## How It Works
9	
10	1. Start an AI coding session (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode)
11	2. When you or the agent run `git commit`, the session data is attached to your commit
12	3. The checkpoint ID is added as a commit trailer. For example:
13	
14	```
15	feat: Add user authentication
16	
17	This commit adds OAuth2 login flow with Google and GitHub providers.
18	
19	Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7
20	```
21	
22	4. The session log and other metadata are stored in a checkpoint in the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch
23	5. On your next `git push`, the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch will be automatically pushed too
24	
25	## Manual Attach
26	
27	If Entire did not capture a session automatically, you can attach it later:
28	
29	```bash
30	entire session attach <session-id> -a <agent>
31	```
32	
33	This is useful when:
34	
35	- Hooks were not installed when the session started
36	- Hooks failed to fire
37	- The session was research-only and did not produce file changes
38	- The session started in another folder but turned out to be relevant somewhere else
39	
40	`entire session attach` reads the transcript, writes the session into `entire/checkpoints/v1`, and links it to your latest commit.
41	
42	- If the last commit already has an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, the session is added to that checkpoint
43	- If the last commit has no checkpoint yet, Entire creates one and asks whether to amend the commit
44	- In non-interactive flows, Entire prints the `Entire-Checkpoint: ...` trailer so you can add it manually
45	
46	Example:
47	
48	```bash
49	entire session attach 019d6c43-1537-7343-9691-1f8cee04fe59 -a codex -f
50	```
51	
52	## Benefits
53	
54	- **Clean Git history** - No extra commits from Entire
55	- **Safe everywhere** - Can be used on `main` or any branch
56	- **Rewind support** - You can rewind file changes and session state
57	- **Resume support** - You or a coworker can resume a branch / commit session
58	
59	## Best Practices
60	
61	- Make commits at logical stopping points or ask your agent to make granular commits
62	- Use meaningful commit messages—they become checkpoint labels
63	- Commit before major changes if you want a rewind point
64	
65	### Auto-Summarize
66	
67	When enabled, Entire uses AI to automatically generate summaries of your sessions when you commit. These summaries are stored with your checkpoint metadata.
68	
69	```json
70	{
71	  "strategy_options": {
72	    "summarize": {
73	      "enabled": true
74	    }
75	  }
76	}
77	```
78	
79	<Note>
80	  Auto-summarize requires Claude CLI to be installed and authenticated. The
81	  summary generation happens in the background and won't block your commit.
82	</Note>
83	
84	Summaries include:
85	
86	- A brief description of what was accomplished
87	- Key decisions made during the session
88	- Files that were modified
89	
90	## Checkpoint Remote
91	
92	By default, Entire pushes the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch to the same remote as your code. If you want to push checkpoint data to a separate repository, you can configure a checkpoint remote.
93	
94	This is useful for keeping checkpoint data off your main repository on GitHub, centralizing checkpoints across multiple repositories, or separating audit trails from production code.
95	
96	### Setup
97	
98	Configure the checkpoint remote via the CLI:
99	
100	```bash
101	entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:myorg/checkpoints-private
102	```
103	
104	Or add it directly to your settings:
105	
106	```json
107	{
108	  "strategy_options": {
109	    "checkpoint_remote": {
110	      "provider": "github",
111	      "repo": "myorg/checkpoints-private"
112	    }
113	  }
114	}
115	```
116	
117	<Note>
118	  Currently, only `github` is supported as a provider. When using a
119	  checkpoint remote, commit and push
120	  [`.entire/settings.json`](/cli/configuration#project-settings) to your
121	  default branch so entire.io can locate your checkpoint data.
122	</Note>
123	
124	### How It Works
125	
126	When you push code, Entire automatically:
127	
128	1. **Derives the checkpoint URL** — Uses the same protocol (SSH or HTTPS) as your push remote
129	2. **Pushes checkpoints separately** — The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch goes to your checkpoint remote
130	
131	### Fork Detection
132	
133	Entire includes built-in fork detection to prevent contributors from accidentally pushing to an organization's private checkpoint repository.
134	
135	If the push remote owner differs from the checkpoint remote owner, the checkpoint push is **skipped**:
136	
137	- You're pushing to `alice/main-repo` (your fork)
138	- Checkpoint remote is configured as `org/checkpoints-private`
139	- Since `alice` ≠ `org`, checkpoints fall back to your fork's origin
140	
141	This ensures that fork contributors don't need write access to the upstream checkpoint repository.
142	
143	### Error Handling
144	
145	If the checkpoint remote is unreachable, Entire warns you but continues:
146	
147	```
148	[entire] Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to checkpoint remote...
149	[entire] Warning: couldn't sync entire/checkpoints/v1: ...
150	[entire] A checkpoint remote is configured in Entire settings but could not be reached.
151	[entire] Checkpoints are saved locally but not synced. Ensure you have access to the checkpoint remote.
152	```
153	
154	Your main Git push still succeeds. Checkpoint failures are non-blocking.
155	
156	## Troubleshooting
157	
158	### GitLab squash merges
159	
160	By default, GitLab squash merges do not preserve commit trailers from the original commits. This removes the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer that Entire uses to link commits to Checkpoint metadata.
161	
162	To preserve it, configure the Squash commit message template under Settings > Repository > Merge requests.
163	
164	Use a template that includes the squashed commit content, for example:
165	
166	```text
167	%{title} (%{reference})
168	
169	%{all_commits}
170	```
171	
```

## What I found — what checkpoints actually are

From the quickstart (`entire-docs/quickstart.mdx`) and `cli/checkpoints.mdx` + the command source:

**A checkpoint is a record of the prompts, transcript, tool calls, and file changes behind an AI-assisted commit.** Mechanically:
- You work with an agent → you `git commit` → Entire attaches the session to that commit automatically.
- The checkpoint ID becomes a commit trailer: `Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7`.
- The data lives on a separate branch (`entire/checkpoints/v1`) so your working branch stays clean — **no extra commits**.
- Your commit message becomes the checkpoint's label.

**The verbs people actually use** (from the command `Short:` strings):
- `checkpoint list` — list checkpoints on the branch
- `checkpoint` — "Inspect, rewind, and search checkpoints"
- `rewind` — "Browse checkpoints and rewind your session"
- `resume` — "Switch to a branch and resume its session" (you *or a coworker*)
- `search` — "semantic and keyword matching" over past checkpoints
- `recap` — "Summarize recent checkpoint activity"

**When someone uses them** (the best-practices section is the gold): *"Make commits at logical stopping points… use meaningful commit messages—they become checkpoint labels… commit before major changes if you want a rewind point."* The payoff is **rewind** (undo to last good state, including session state) and **resume** (pick up a session with full context).

## The key insight for the game

The quickstart is literally titled **"create your first checkpoint."** Checkpoints are *the* foundational Entire concept — the first thing a real user does. So making **Level 1 = "create your first checkpoint"** is pedagogically perfect and matches the official onboarding.

And here's the narrative gift: **a checkpoint stores the *intent* (the prompt + reasoning), not just the diff.** A plain git commit recovers *what* changed; a checkpoint recovers *what you were trying to do and why.* That maps *exactly* onto your fiction — the ship has amnesia, and a checkpoint crystal is the only thing that survives it, because it stores **memory/context, not just state.** Lean into that; it's what makes it Entire and not just git.

## Gamification directions

I'll frame each as **mechanic → how you win → how you score / beat someone**, since those are your three open questions.

**A. Save-discipline (teaches *when* to checkpoint)**
- *Mechanic:* you perform repair actions on the ship (small "file changes"). You choose when to drop a checkpoint crystal. Then a **memory storm** hits and wipes everything uncommitted — only checkpointed progress survives.
- *Win:* restore the ship's memory chain to working order → it powers on → escape.
- *Score / compete:* a **recoverability score** — how much progress survived the storm. Rewards judgment, not volume (spamming meaningless crystals should be *penalized*, mirroring "meaningful messages at logical stopping points"). Leaderboard on score; head-to-head = same crash, fewer losses wins.

**B. Rewind-to-last-good (teaches *recovery* — this was your original puzzle #2)**
- *Mechanic:* a corruption spreads through the memory chain. You read crystal labels to find the **last good one before the corruption** and rewind to it.
- *Win:* rewind to exactly the right point — purge the corruption without losing good work.
- *Score / compete:* **precision + speed.** Over-rewind (lose good work) or under-rewind (keep the bug) both cost points; good labels let you find it fast → time bonus. Speedrun leaderboard.

**C. Resume / co-op relay (teaches the *team* superpower)**
- *Mechanic:* you inherit a half-finished memory chain from "another astronaut" and must `resume` — read their last checkpoint's context to continue without redoing their work.
- *Win:* finish the repair using their recovered context.
- *Score:* fewest redundant actions (you didn't repeat what they already did). This is the most uniquely-Entire mechanic (git can't do it).

## My read

For **Level 1**, I'd go with **A (creating checkpoints) as the spine, with a light touch of B (rewind) as the climax** — that mirrors the quickstart arc (*make a change → checkpoint it → view/rewind it*) and front-loads the foundational skill. Save full **rewind precision** for level 2 and **resume/co-op** for a later level.

The single scoring number that ties it together and answers "beat someone else": a **Recoverability Score** — *how much of your work could you get back when disaster struck?* It's the real-world value of checkpoints, expressed as one comparable number.

**One design trap to flag:** don't reward checkpoint *volume*, or you'll teach people to spam commits. Reward *well-placed, well-labeled* checkpoints — that's the actual skill.

A couple of open questions worth chewing on:
- **Is the "memory storm wipes uncommitted work" framing fair/fun, or too punishing?** (Alternative: no wipe, just a recoverability *rating* at the end — gentler.)
- **Solo score + async leaderboard, or real head-to-head?** Async (ghost/leaderboard) is far simpler to build and still scratches the competition itch.

Want me to sketch the Level 1 loop in detail for one of these directions, or keep widening the idea space?

> AGENT

Pure creation it is — no rewind, no resume. That actually sharpens the level, because it lets you teach the *one* thing the quickstart teaches: **make your first checkpoint, and make it well.** Here's how a creation-only level can still be a real game with a win and a score.

## The core mechanic, made physical

In real Entire you don't "make a checkpoint" directly — you **commit**, and the checkpoint forms, capturing *everything since your last one* (prompts, changes, intent). That detail is the whole game:

> **A crystal captures everything that happened since the last crystal.**

So *when* you choose to checkpoint decides what each memory *contains*:
- Wait too long → one bloated crystal swallows five unrelated things → a confusing, useless memory.
- Drop one at each clean beat → a legible chain the ship can actually read back.

That's the lesson ("commit at logical stopping points") turned into a physical decision, with zero rewind involved.

## The Level 1 loop (creation only)

1. You do repair work on the ship — a sequence of distinct tasks (patch hull → restore oxygen → reroute power → calibrate nav). These are the "file changes."
2. **You** decide when to seal a memory crystal, and **you label it.** The crystal absorbs the span of work since your last one and shows you what it captured — *what* you did and the *intent* behind it.
3. No undo. You just keep going, building the chain.

## How you win

At the end, **the ship plays its memory back from your chain** to reboot. If the chain is coherent — clean spans, meaningful labels — the AI narrates its own restored story, remembers who it is, and powers on → **escape.** A sloppy chain still boots, but the AI's recollection is garbled and full of holes ("…I don't remember anything between *power* and *nav*…"). Winning = the ship remembers itself. No hard-lose needed.

## How you score / beat someone

One number — call it **Memory Integrity** (or Recall Score) — built from creation quality only:

- **Granularity** — did your crystal boundaries line up with the real task boundaries? One giant crystal across all four tasks scores low; ~one per task scores high.
- **Label quality** — "Restored oxygen scrubbers" beats "stuff" / "wip" / "asdf."
- **Coverage** — any task that fell into a gap with no crystal = a hole in the ship's memory.
- **Signal-to-noise** — empty/junk crystals (committing nothing meaningful) cost points.

Because the scenario is the same sequence for everyone, those roll up to a **comparable score → leaderboard**, and head-to-head is just "same ship, higher integrity wins." This directly rewards the real skill — *judgment about when and how to checkpoint* — and deliberately does **not** reward volume, so it can't teach checkpoint-spam.

**The one trap to keep in mind:** granularity has to be scoreable, so the scenario needs clear natural "logical units" (the four named tasks). The ideal answer is roughly one well-labeled crystal per task — that's what the score measures you against.

- **Should missing a checkpoint be visible in the moment** (you feel the gap forming), or only revealed at the end when the ship reads back its memory?

**Simplest true thing about a checkpoint: it's a save point. You do something that matters, you save it, it's remembered forever.**

So the whole level is just that, no extra machinery:

- Restore enough memories → the ship remembers itself → you escape. **That's the win.**

No rewind, no spans, no granularity math. Just: *do a thing → checkpoint it → it's saved forever.* The lesson the player walks away with is the only one that matters at first — **"a checkpoint saves your moment so it's never lost."**

If you want a score later, it's the obvious one: how many memories you recovered (or how fast). But that's optional polish, not the core.

> DEVELOPER

which do you think..automatic or manual

> AGENT

**Manual** — and not just for game-feel reasons; it's actually truer to Entire.

Two reasons:

1. **The level is about creating checkpoints, so the player should create one.** If it's automatic they just watch it happen — the one verb the level exists to teach never passes through their hands. Manual makes them *feel* the act, so it sticks.

2. **It mirrors real Entire better than automatic does.** The capture is automatic, yes — but the human still makes a deliberate choice: *"this is a moment worth committing."* The player pressing the key to save **is** that decision. So manual teaches the real instinct ("I just did something meaningful — save it"), which is the whole habit you want them to leave with.

Automatic would only win if the goal were "checkpoints happen invisibly, don't worry about them" — but that's the opposite of a level meant to make the concept land.

So: **player presses a key to checkpoint after a meaningful moment, and watches that memory get permanently restored to the ship.** Deliberate choice, automatic capture.

116	let current = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("view") === "island"
117	  ? islandView : planetView;
118	current.enter();
119	
120	// ---------- fade transition ----------
121	const fade = document.getElementById("fade");
122	const hint = document.getElementById("hint");
123	let transitioning = false;
124	hint.classList.toggle("hidden", current !== planetView);
125	
126	function switchTo(view) {
127	  if (transitioning || view === current) return;
128	  transitioning = true;
129	  fade.classList.add("show");
130	  setTimeout(() => {
131	    current.exit();
132	    current = view;
133	    current.enter();
134	    hint.classList.toggle("hidden", current !== planetView);
135	    fade.classList.remove("show");
136	    transitioning = false;
137	  }, 650); // match #fade CSS transition
138	}
139	
140	// ---------- resize ----------
141	window.addEventListener("resize", () => {
142	  renderer.setSize(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight);
143	  planetView.resize();
144	  islandView.resize();
145	});
146	
147	// ---------- loop ----------
148	const clock = new THREE.Clock();
149	let firstFrame = true;
150	
151	function animate() {
152	  const dt = Math.min(clock.getDelta(), 0.05); // clamp big tab-switch jumps
153	  const t = clock.elapsedTime;
154	  current.update(dt, t);
155	  renderer.render(current.scene, current.camera);
156	
157	  if (firstFrame) {
158	    firstFrame = false;
159	    document.getElementById("loader").classList.add("done");
160	  }
161	  requestAnimationFrame(animate);
162	}
163	animate();
164

4	function makeHaloTexture(color = "#6fe3ff") {

136	// Convert lat/lon (degrees) to a point on a sphere of the given radius.
137	function latLonToVec3(lat, lon, radius) {
138	  const phi = (90 - lat) * (Math.PI / 180);
139	  const theta = (lon + 180) * (Math.PI / 180);
140	  return new THREE.Vector3(
141	    -radius * Math.sin(phi) * Math.cos(theta),
142	    radius * Math.cos(phi),
143	    radius * Math.sin(phi) * Math.sin(theta)
144	  );
145	}
146	
147	/**
148	 * Build debris anchors on the planet surface. Returns the group (to add to the
149	 * planet so they rotate together) and the list of pickable meshes for
150	 * raycasting, each carrying its fragment data in userData.
151	 */
152	export function createDebris(planetRadius) {
153	  const group = new THREE.Group();
154	  const pickables = [];
155	
156	  for (const frag of FRAGMENTS) {
157	    const pos = latLonToVec3(frag.lat, frag.lon, planetRadius);
158	    const anchor = new THREE.Group();
159	    anchor.position.copy(pos);
160	    // Orient so local +Y points away from the planet centre.
161	    anchor.quaternion.setFromUnitVectors(
162	      new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0),
163	      pos.clone().normalize()
164	    );
165	
166	    const model = BUILDERS[frag.kind]();
167	    model.position.y = 0.02;
168	
169	    // Halo to make it findable; doubles as the click target (big & flat).
170	    const halo = new THREE.Mesh(
171	      new THREE.PlaneGeometry(0.34, 0.34),
172	      new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({
173	        map: haloTexture(),
174	        transparent: true,
175	        blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending,
176	        depthWrite: false,
177	        opacity: 0.9,
178	      })
179	    );
180	    halo.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2;
181	    halo.position.y = 0.005;
182	
183	    anchor.add(halo, model);
184	    anchor.userData = { fragment: frag, halo, model, baseScale: 1 };
185	    group.add(anchor);
186	    pickables.push(anchor);
187	  }
188	
189	  return { group, pickables };
190	}
191

1	import * as THREE from "three";
2	import { PointerLockControls } from "three/addons/controls/PointerLockControls.js";
3	
4	// First-person walker: PointerLockControls for mouse-look + keyboard movement
5	// that hugs the terrain. Click the canvas to look around; Escape releases the mouse.
6	
7	export function createFirstPerson(camera, domElement, {
8	  heightAt,
9	  radius = 80,        // keep the walker on the island, not out at sea
10	  eyeHeight = 2.4,
11	  speed = 22,         // world units / second
12	} = {}) {
13	  const controls = new PointerLockControls(camera, domElement);
14	
15	  const keys = { f: false, b: false, l: false, r: false };
16	  function onKey(down) {
17	    return (e) => {
18	      switch (e.code) {
19	        case "KeyW": case "ArrowUp": keys.f = down; break;
20	        case "KeyS": case "ArrowDown": keys.b = down; break;
21	        case "KeyA": case "ArrowLeft": keys.l = down; break;
22	        case "KeyD": case "ArrowRight": keys.r = down; break;
23	        default: return;
24	      }
25	      // Don't let arrow keys scroll the page while walking.
26	      if (down) e.preventDefault();
27	    };
28	  }
29	  const onKeyDown = onKey(true);
30	  const onKeyUp = onKey(false);
31	
32	  // Place the walker on the ground at a given (x, z).
33	  function groundAt(x, z) {
34	    camera.position.set(x, heightAt(x, z) + eyeHeight, z);
35	  }
36	
37	  function update(dt) {
38	    if (controls.isLocked) {
39	      const d = speed * dt;
40	      // Forward/back and strafe are horizontal; height is re-applied below.
41	      if (keys.f) controls.moveForward(d);
42	      if (keys.b) controls.moveForward(-d);
43	      if (keys.r) controls.moveRight(d);
44	      if (keys.l) controls.moveRight(-d);
45	
46	      // Clamp to the island so you can't walk off into the sea.
47	      const p = camera.position;
48	      const dist = Math.hypot(p.x, p.z);
49	      if (dist > radius) {
50	        const s = radius / dist;
51	        p.x *= s; p.z *= s;
52	      }
53	    }
54	    // Always glue the eye to the terrain (even while standing still after a
55	    // teleport/reset), so the ground never clips through the camera.
56	    camera.position.y = heightAt(camera.position.x, camera.position.z) + eyeHeight;
57	  }
58	
59	  function attach() {
60	    window.addEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown);
61	    window.addEventListener("keyup", onKeyUp);
62	  }
63	  function detach() {
64	    window.removeEventListener("keydown", onKeyDown);
65	    window.removeEventListener("keyup", onKeyUp);
66	    keys.f = keys.b = keys.l = keys.r = false;
67	  }
68	
69	  return {
70	    controls,
71	    update,
72	    groundAt,
73	    attach,
74	    detach,
75	    lock: () => controls.lock(),
76	    unlock: () => controls.unlock(),
77	    get isLocked() { return controls.isLocked; },
78	  };
79	}
80

Verification caught a real bug. In the **before** screenshot, the "✓ Checkpoint created" confirmation is showing *at the same time* as the "Create checkpoint" button — before anything was clicked. The probe confirmed it: `OFFER_VISIBLE: true` **and** `DONE_VISIBLE: true`.

Cause: `#ckpt-done { display: flex }` is an ID selector (specificity 1,0,0) which beats `.hidden { display: none }` (0,1,0), so `.hidden` can't hide it. Let me fix the specificity:

}

It's built and verified working. Here's what I implemented and what the verification found.

## What's in now

The "you just did something → want to checkpoint it?" flow, wired into the existing inspect-an-artifact moment:

1. Walk up to an artifact, press **E** → the inspection panel opens as before.
2. Below the lore, it now offers: **"You just recovered a lost memory."** with your explainer copy — *"Create a checkpoint to keep it. A checkpoint saves a core memory — every step you took to recover this — so the ship can never lose it again."* — and a **Create checkpoint** button.
3. Click it → the offer flips to a **✓ "Checkpoint created · Core memory restored to the ship"** confirmation, and the footer counter ticks up (`core memories restored · 1/4`). Restore all four and it reads *"all core memories restored · the ship remembers itself"* — your no-rewind win condition.

Creating the checkpoint is also what dims the artifact's beam now (it used to dim the instant you looked), so the world reflects what you've actually *saved*, not just seen.

**Files touched:** `index.html` (panel markup), `src/main.js` (panel rendering + create-button wiring + progress counter), `src/islandView.js` (passes the checkpoint context on E, treats "collected" = "checkpointed"), `src/style.css` (checkpoint block styling).

## Verification (drove the real game in a browser)

I walked a first-person player to an artifact, pressed E, and clicked the button — screenshots above are the actual before/after. It **caught one real bug**: `#ckpt-done { display: flex }` is an ID selector that out-specificity'd `.hidden { display: none }`, so the "✓ Checkpoint created" confirmation was showing *before* you clicked anything (both states visible at once). Fixed with `#ckpt-done:not(.hidden)` and re-verified — confirmed deterministically (the hidden element now computes `display: none`) and visually.

Two notes, neither blocking:
- Nothing here is committed yet — it's all in the working tree alongside the pre-existing untracked `.codex/` and `HANDOFF.md`.
- The win state is currently just the footer line. When you want, the natural next beat is making that fourth checkpoint *feel* like an ending (the ship boots / escape).
